issues.legal_issue: A child witness who can understand questions and give rational answers may provide the basis for a conviction, although corroboration is a prudent safeguard rather than a legal requirement.
material_facts: The prosecution case rested principally on the testimony of the deceased’s approximately ten-year-old daughter, who said she witnessed the assault.
The courts below found her competent and reliable, and the Supreme Court found her testimony unblemished and saw no likelihood of tutoring.
Other evidence, including testimony about her presence near the scene and medical evidence, corroborated material aspects of her account.
issues.conclusion: A child witness’s testimony can by itself support a conviction if the witness is competent and reliable; corroboration is desirable as a matter of prudence but is not invariably required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 118 of the Indian Evidence Act permits a child to testify if the child can understand the questions and give rational answers; the testimony’s credibility depends on the circumstances of the case. The court should assess reliability and the possibility of tutoring, and it is prudent to seek corroboration from dependable evidence, but corroboration is not a mandatory condition for conviction. No earlier cases are identified in the judgment as authority for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_trial and child_understands_questions and child_gives_rational_answers and child_testimony_reliable and not likelihood_of_tutoring

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution relies on a child’s testimony.
predicates.child_understands_questions: The child witness can understand the questions put to them.
predicates.child_gives_rational_answers: The child witness can give rational answers to those questions.
predicates.child_testimony_reliable: The court finds the child witness’s testimony reliable in the circumstances of the case.
predicates.likelihood_of_tutoring: The child witness is likely to have been tutored.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial relies on a child who understands questions, gives rational answers, and is a reliable witness without a likelihood of tutoring, the child’s testimony can support a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction supported by a reliable eyewitness account and corroborating evidence may be sustained when an appellate court has set aside an acquittal on that evidence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged convictions imposed after the High Court dismissed one accused’s appeal and allowed the State’s appeal against the acquittal of the other two accused.
The child eyewitness said all three accused attacked the deceased with axes and a sickle, and the Supreme Court accepted her account as reliable.
The eyewitness’s presence near the scene was corroborated by other witnesses’ accounts of the events and their movements after the assault.
The first information report named all three accused as assailants.
The medical evidence recorded sixteen injuries and was consistent with an assault involving different weapons and the eyewitness’s account.
The prosecution’s evidence about recovery of weapons was not accepted by the trial court and was not relied on by the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittals, and the convictions were upheld; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court assessed the evidence as a whole, including the reliable child eyewitness’s account, corroboration of her presence and the prompt report naming the assailants, and medical evidence consistent with her account. It held that the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittals and upheld the convictions. The judgment cites no earlier cases for a distinct rule governing appellate reversal of acquittals.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction_after_appellate_reversal_of_acquittal and reliable_eyewitness_account and eyewitness_presence_corroborated and prompt_report_names_accused and medical_evidence_consistent

predicates.appeal_against_conviction_after_appellat: The proceeding is an appeal against convictions entered after an appellate court set aside acquittals.
predicates.reliable_eyewitness_account: An eyewitness gives an account that the court finds reliable.
predicates.eyewitness_presence_corroborated: Other evidence corroborates the eyewitness’s presence near the scene at the relevant time.
predicates.prompt_report_names_accused: A prompt report identifies the accused as the assailants.
predicates.medical_evidence_consistent: Medical evidence is consistent with material aspects of the eyewitness’s account.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges convictions entered after acquittals were set aside, and a reliable eyewitness account is corroborated as to presence, promptly identifies the accused, and is consistent with the medical evidence, the convictions are upheld and the reversal of acquittals is sustained.
